messages.subject: Re: How can I use the key as an index?
parts:
Hi rmx,
first I approved only one of your last three messages as they seem duplicates. As explained on our group main page, every user's first message to the group is moderated to prevent spam. From now on your messages should be published in a timely fashion. As to the specific question, without more code and more detail on what you are trying to do I am going to make an educated guess and say "both". You need to add explicit row information and you need to use it as key. So for instance if you represent your matrix as  records keyval(row, c(val1, val2)) and you want to do a transpose, the program would look like

mapreduce(input, 
  map = function(row,vals) lapply(seq_along(v), function(i) keyval(i, list(col = k, val = v[i]))),
  reduce = function(row, vals) keyval(row, vals$val[order(vals$col)]),
  to.data.frame = T)

or something of that sort (I haven't even checked this is syntactically correct).
This is a bit of a demo code, speed won't be that great and  I think if you have such skinny matrices it will be a challenge to make it much more efficient.  If I were working on something like this, I would explore a submatrix representation (row.offset, col.offset, submatrix), where the position is in the submatrix can be translated into the larger matrix by summing the offset.  So the transpose becomes

mapreduce(input,
  map = function(k, submat) keyval(NULL, list(row.offset = submat$col.offset, col.offset = submat$row.offset, submatrix = t(submat$submatrix)))

Again sorry for the sketchy code. You see here that the transpose is a map-only job, no reduce part, which is a big performance advantage. Of course we are  not trying to do only transpose, but it is at least one vote for this representation. Plus we have control on the size of the submatrix, independent on how skinny or fat the data is. That means we have a much better chance of achieving a fast implementation, by leveraging vectorized operations in R such as t(). My next step would be to implement matrix multiplication and see how that looks and performs. I hope this helps


Antonio


On Thursday, June 7, 2012 5:28:24 AM UTC-7, rmx wrote:
Hello,

I want to have an indexed dataset. Lets say, the dataset is a matrix M with two columns (val1, val2). 

index   val1 val2
1        3.14   3.11
2      23.23  1.12
...
n      n-val1 n-val2

I want to get the value for a certain index x:
V(x)=M[x,] 

Using R in local mode this is straightforward, since the matrix is automatically indexed. When uploading to HDFS, the index is lost. I could add another column and fill it with a sequence of numbers to indexing it.
Since HDFS and MapReduce has the key concept. Can I use the key for indexing?
If so, how?

Thanks
RMX

messages.author: 6ac7e7dfbe4f6c38
messages.subject: Re: [RHadoop:#122] Re: How can I use the key as an index?
parts:
The transpose was just to give you an idea of how to use an explicit index. to.dfs on a matrix does some conversion to a list of rows that may or may not be the best approach for most uses. I'd suggest you convert a matrix to a list of key-value pairs with explicit index and then write it to disk. It is  not obvious, you have to implement it. It could make a nice contribution to rmr.


Antonio

Hi,

I just come across HBASE.
I never experienced that. Maybe that suits more my needs.
I have to make a program that iterates through a dataset and calculate
distances between all the points X and a smaller set of points Y (that
belongs to X). At the end of each iteration, a new Y is selected
according to the calculated distances. The new selected Y will be used
to calculate new distances with X.
Maybe the dataset could be replicated in HDFS and HBASE. Then the
program could load the values of Y from HBASE and mapreduce the
distances over the X in HDFS.

Would this be more performance?
What do you think?

Thanks,
Rui

Hi,

I just come across HBASE.
I never experienced that. Maybe that suits more my needs.
I have to make a program that iterates through a dataset and calculate
distances between all the points X and a smaller set of points Y (that
belongs to X). At the end  of each iteration, a new Y is selected
according to the calculated distances. The new selected Y will be used
to calculate new distances with X.
Maybe the dataset could be replicated in HDFS and HBASE. Then the
program could  load the values of Y from HBASE  and  mapreduce the
distances over the X in HDFS.

Would this be more performance?

In some use cases, yes, in others, no. One is a database, the other a batch processing system. They have different goals and good reasons why they both exist.
 
What do you think?

It seems like your problem is very similar to k-means. Take a look at the implementation in the Tutorial. Y would have to fit in main memory for that approach to apply. You can run mapreduce directly on hbase tables, we have an issue open to make that possible in rmr, lessening the need for duplicating data sets. Giving me information about the size of X and Y would be helpful. Also read about equijoin.
 
Antonio

Thanks,
Rui
